title: NASA issues long-awaited call to industry for private space stations
gist: NASA released a 360-page request for proposals for commercial low-Earth-orbit space stations to succeed the ISS as early as 2030, with responses due December 8 and a decision in April. The RFP offers to furnish crew transport for the first four NASA missions, priced at $325 million per crew flight and $300 million per cargo flight, in light of SpaceX planning to retire Crew Dragon.

themes.theme: NASA commercial station RFP timeline and structure

insights.claim: NASA issued a 360-page RFP for private LEO space stations to succeed the ISS as early as 2030, with responses due December 8, selection of two or more contractors in this phase, and a final decision in April.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Sets the near-term catalyst calendar for commercial space station bidders.

insights.claim: Phase 1 winners are guaranteed at least $100 million; Phase 2 starting next year funds development and certification, and Phase 3 buys at least four NASA astronaut missions, with future phases worth billions.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Defines how funding scales from tens of millions to billions, relevant to commercial space valuations.

insights.claim: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit and sees commercial stations as freeing NASA resources for Moon and Mars missions.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Signals sustained government anchor-customer demand for LEO.
insights.quote: We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit

insights.claim: Likely bidders include Axiom Space, Voyager Space (Starlab) and Vast Space; Blue Origin won an earlier round of funding but doubts remain about its commitment, and SpaceX appears unlikely to bid for now.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: SpaceX’s absence leaves a smaller field; watch which firms are selected for Phase 1.

insights.claim: Bidders signaled confidence: Voyager’s CEO called Starlab the strongest plan, Axiom cited its human spaceflight experience, and Vast said it is in final integration with Haven-1.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Company statements are promotional; Haven-1 readiness is a milestone to monitor.

insights.claim: SpaceX plans to retire Crew Dragon as soon as possible, almost certainly when the ISS deorbits in 2030 or 2032, and has not offered to sell seats to private station operators, creating a transport gap for station providers.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Crew access is the critical bottleneck for commercial stations and favors alternative providers like Boeing.

insights.claim: To address the gap, NASA gave Boeing an additional $359 million two weeks ago to certify Starliner, and the RFP does not require bidders to show a signed contract or letter of intent with a transport provider.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Government support lowers Boeing Starliner’s program risk and lowers the barrier for station bidders.

insights.claim: NASA offers to furnish transportation for the first four NASA service missions, likely by brokering deals between station firms and Boeing, and estimates a 2030 four-seat crew flight at $325 million and a cargo flight at $300 million.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Explicit price anchors of $325 million and $300 million per flight inform the economics of station operations.
